lesson.title: Efficiency and power in a drive

lead.text: The first job is to measure how quickly a machine delivers energy. Take a winch that raises a 500 N crate by 3 m. The work done is the force times the distance, 500 × 3 = 1,500 J, and that is the same whether the winch takes five seconds or fifty. The difference between those two jobs is how hard the winch has to work.

The quantity that tells them apart is power, the work done each second. If the winch takes 5 s, its power is 1,500 ÷ 5 = 300 J per second. One joule per second is one watt, written W, so that is 300 W. The same number comes more directly from the speed. The crate rises 3 m in 5 s, which is 0.6 m/s, and force × speed = 500 × 0.6 = 300 W.

afterFigure.text: So in a straight line, power is force times speed. A winch that lifts the same crate twice as fast delivers twice the power, because it does the same work in half the time.

lead.text: Use force times speed. The winch in the question lifts at a steady rate, so one second of its work is enough.

A motor does not lift anything in a straight line. Its shaft turns, so its speed is given in revolutions per minute and its push is a torque. To get a power from those two, the speed of turning has to be written in a unit that fits with torque.

That unit uses the radian. Take a wheel of radius r and lay a piece of string of length r along its rim. The angle that string covers at the centre is one radian, a little under 60°. A full turn is the whole circumference, 2π × r, so it is 2π radians, about 6.28. The rate of turning in radians per second is the angular speed, written ω, the Greek letter omega.
To change rpm into rad/s, multiply by 2π, because each revolution is 2π radians, and divide by 60, because a minute has 60 seconds. A shaft at 120 rpm has ω = 120 × 2π ÷ 60 = 12.57 rad/s.
Each revolution is 2π radians, and a minute is 60 seconds. Put those two facts together.

steps.headline: The power of a turning shaft

lead.text: The winch idea carries over to a shaft. Picture a force F pushing round the rim of a wheel of radius r. The torque is F × r. When the shaft turns at ω radians per second, a point on the rim travels a distance r × ω each second, because a radian is the angle whose arc is as long as the radius.
Power is force times speed, so the power is F × rω. Regroup that as (F × r) × ω and it is the torque times the angular speed: P = T × ω.

afterFigure.text: Take a torque of 5 N·m at 120 rpm. The angular speed of 12.57 rad/s gives 5 × 12.57 ≈ 63 W. The radian is why the formula needs no extra factors, so the speed must be converted first. Putting 120 in directly would give 600, nearly ten times too large.

lead.text: The question gives the speed in rpm. The figure shows two motors with the same torque and different speeds.

steps.headline: A motor delivers 8 N·m at 3,000 rpm. Find its power output.

lead.text: Here is the same method for another motor.

workedSteps.text: Convert rpm to radians per second.

lead.text: So far every shaft has passed on all of its power. A real mesh does not. The teeth rub as they roll over each other, and some of the work turns into heat and wear. Engineers describe this with efficiency, the fraction of the power put in that comes out as useful power. A mesh with an efficiency of 0.95, or 95%, passes on 95 W of every 100 W it receives.

A gearbox usually has several meshes in a row, and each pair of gears is called a stage. Each stage takes its share of what the one before delivered. Two stages at 90% leave 90% of 90%, which is 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.81, or 81%. Taking 10% off twice would give 80%, which is wrong, because the second loss applies to what is left after the first.

afterFigure.text: The efficiencies multiply, so each added stage costs a few more per cent. That is the price of the extra torque. A third reduction stage lets the same motor turn the output with more torque, at a lower output speed and with a little less of the power arriving.

steps.headline: A gearbox has two meshes, each 95% efficient. Find the overall efficiency.

lead.text: Any number of stages multiply in the same way.

workedSteps.text: Each mesh passes on 0.95 of the power it receives.
Multiply the two efficiencies, then give the answer as a percentage.

lead.text: Losses change the output torque and leave the speed alone. The teeth still pass at the same rate, so a 4 : 1 gearbox still turns its output at exactly a quarter of the input speed, whatever the friction. The tooth counts fix the speed ratio.

Less power out at the same speed means less torque, since power is torque times speed. So the real output torque is the ideal output torque times the efficiency. Take 10 N·m going into a 3 : 1 pair that is 80% efficient. The ideal output is 10 × 3 = 30 N·m, and the real one is 30 × 0.8 = 24 N·m.
Find the ideal torque first, then take away what the losses cost.

The losses decide how big a motor to buy. The load receives only the useful power, and the motor supplies that plus whatever is lost on the way. So the motor has to supply the useful power divided by the machine's efficiency. A load that needs 600 W through a machine that is 75% efficient takes 600 ÷ 0.75 = 800 W from the motor, which is more than the load receives.

The same reasoning applies to force. A block and tackle with 4 strands has an ideal mechanical advantage of 4, but friction in the pulleys means some of the effort is wasted. The real mechanical advantage is the ideal one times the efficiency. At 75% that is 4 × 0.75 = 3, so a 900 N load needs an effort of 900 ÷ 3 = 300 N, where the ideal answer would have been 225 N.
Work out the power at the hook first. The motor must supply more than that.

lesson.orientation: Follow the energy from a hoist's load back to its motor, and find the power, torque and motor size once friction takes its share.
lesson.reviewLabel: Efficiency and power in a drive
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Put a hand on the casing of a gearbox that has been running for an hour and it is warm. The warmth is energy that went in at one end and never came out at the other. The teeth rub as they slide past each other, the bearings drag, and all that friction turns some of the motor's work into heat.

The last lesson let a pair of gears pass on everything it was given. That was a fair way to learn the rule, but a real machine always pays something, and the payment decides which motor you need to buy. Take a hoist that lifts a heavy load through a gearbox and a pulley. The motor has to supply the lift and the heat.

This lesson follows the energy from the load back to the motor. It first measures how quickly energy is delivered, in a straight line and then in a turning shaft. It then counts what each gear pair takes, and finishes by sizing the motor.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find what a turning shaft delivers, and the torque and motor size a real drive needs once friction takes its share.

recap.keyIdea: Power is torque times angular speed, with the speed in radians per second. Efficiencies multiply, and the motor supplies the useful power divided by the efficiency.

blocks.text: You started with a warm gearbox and followed the energy back from the hook. A shaft at 20 N·m and 1,500 rpm delivers 3,142 W once the speed is converted to 157.08 rad/s. Two meshes at 95% pass on 90.25% of the power, and a 90% efficient 4 : 1 gearbox gives 72 N·m.
For the hoist, lifting 2,000 N at 0.5 m/s is 1,000 W at the hook, so an 80% efficient system needs a motor that supplies 1,250 W. The heat in the casing is the difference.

recap.nextHook: You can now follow a force from a load back through pulleys and gears to a motor shaft, and say what each part keeps. Pick any machine and ask where the force goes and how much is lost on the way.

questions.prompt: A winch lifts a 600 N weight at a steady 2 m/s. How many watts is it delivering?
hints: Power is the work done each second.
Work is force times distance.
Multiply the force by the distance covered each second.
questions.onCorrect: 1,200 W. Power is force times speed. For a turning shaft the same idea becomes torque times angular speed.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the force by the speed. Power is force times speed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each second the winch raises 600 N by 2 m, which is 1,200 J per second: 1,200 W.

questions.prompt: Convert 60 rpm to radians per second, to two decimal places.
hints: One revolution is 2π radians.
Divide by 60 to turn minutes into seconds.
Calculate 60 × 2π ÷ 60.
questions.onCorrect: 6.28 rad/s: one turn per second is 2π radians per second.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves the speed in rpm. Multiply by 2π and divide by 60.
That multiplies by 2π but does not divide by 60.

questions.prompt: A motor delivers 20 N·m at 1,500 rpm. Find its power output in watts, to the nearest watt.
hints: Convert rpm to radians per second: multiply by 2π and divide by 60.
Power is torque times angular speed.
Calculate 20 × 1,500 × 2π ÷ 60 and round.
questions.onCorrect: About 3,142 W: torque times angular speed, with the speed in radians per second.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies torque by speed in rpm. Convert rpm to radians per second first.

questions.prompt: Why convert 3,000 rpm to radians per second before multiplying by the torque?
hints: What unit of speed makes torque × speed come out in watts?
questions.onCorrect: N·m times rad/s gives watts. With rpm the answer would be wrong by a large factor.

misconceptions.feedback: Rpm is a perfectly good speed. It just is not the unit that gives watts.
Torque is in newton metres. The radians belong to the speed.

choices.label: Watts need the speed in radians per second, not revolutions per minute.
Because rpm is not a measure of speed.
Because torque is measured in radians.

acceptedIdeas: Watts need the speed in radians per second, not revolutions per minute.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Watts need the speed in radians per second, not revolutions per minute.. Torque in N·m times speed in rad/s gives watts.

questions.prompt: Three stages are each 90% efficient. Find the overall efficiency as a percentage.
hints: Each stage passes on a fraction of what it receives.
Multiply the stage efficiencies as decimals.
Calculate 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9, then convert to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: 72.9%: each stage keeps 90% of what it gets, so the fractions multiply.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts 10% three times. Each stage passes on 90% of what it receives, so multiply.
That is one stage. There are three, and their efficiencies multiply.

questions.prompt: Find the overall efficiency as a percentage.
hints: Write each stage as a decimal.
Multiply the two efficiencies.
Calculate 0.95 × 0.95, then convert to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: 90.25%: multiplying keeps track of the power left after each stage.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts 5% twice. Each stage passes on 95% of what it receives, so multiply.
That is one stage. There are two, and their efficiencies multiply.

questions.prompt: A single-stage gearbox with a 4 : 1 reduction is 90% efficient. The input torque is 20 N·m. Find the output torque in N·m.
hints: Start from the ideal torque multiplication.
Losses reduce torque because the speed ratio is fixed by the teeth.
Calculate 20 × 4 × 0.9.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ideal output 20 × 4 = 80 N·m; with losses 80 × 0.9 = 72 N·m.

questions.onCorrect: 72 N·m: the ideal torque times the efficiency, since the speed ratio is fixed by the teeth.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the ideal torque. Losses reduce it.
That applies the efficiency but not the 4 : 1 ratio.

questions.prompt: A hoist lifts 2,000 N at 0.5 m/s through a pulley system that is 80% efficient overall. Find the power the motor must supply, in watts.
hints: Useful power is force times speed.
Input power is useful power divided by efficiency.
questions.onCorrect: 1,250 W: the motor supplies the useful power divided by the efficiency.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the useful power at the hook. Losses mean the motor supplies more.
That multiplies by the efficiency. The motor supplies more than the hook receives, so divide.

questions.prompt: A block and tackle with 4 supporting strands is 80% efficient. Find the effort needed to raise a 1,600 N load, in N.
hints: The ideal effort is load divided by the number of strands.
Friction means the real effort is larger: divide by the efficiency too.
questions.onCorrect: 500 N: the real mechanical advantage is the ideal 4 times the efficiency.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the ideal effort. Friction makes the real effort bigger.
That multiplies by the efficiency. Friction raises the effort, so divide.

questions.prompt: A designer adds a third reduction stage so that the same motor delivers more output torque. What is given up?
hints: Output power can never exceed input power.

acceptedIdeas: Output speed, plus a little extra loss
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Output speed, plus a little extra loss. More reduction multiplies torque by slowing the output, and each extra mesh wastes more power.

choices.label: Output speed, plus a little extra loss

questions.onCorrect: More reduction multiplies torque by slowing the output, and each extra mesh wastes a few more per cent of the power.

misconceptions.feedback: The motor sets the input power. A third stage changes what the output does with it.
Torque is never free. More torque costs speed, and each stage adds loss.
